name: Gum massage (Stillman technique)

card.summary: A gumline brushing/gum-massage method; little evidence was found in the sources reviewed.
card.note: Hard pressure on gums is cautioned against in general guidance.

quick.overview:
The Stillman technique is a brushing method involving gentle gumline action, sometimes described as gum massage.

No trial evidence was found in the sources reviewed.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say stimulating the gums improves circulation and plaque removal at the gumline.
quick.risks: General guidance cautions against pressing hard on teeth and gums.

lead: The Stillman technique is a toothbrushing method in which the brush is angled at the gumline and moved with vertical motions above and below it, so the bristles both clean the necks of the teeth and stimulate the gums. It is similar to the Bass method, and a modified Stillman version is described in dental literature.[2][3] People use it, and gum massage more broadly, to keep gums firm, pink and free of plaque-related swelling, which supports a healthier-looking smile.
Gum massage can mean brushing technique, finger massage, or massage with oils or herbal powders. Trials have examined each of these in gum-health settings rather than for cosmetic outcomes.[3][4][5]

Wikipedia notes that technique advice from dental associations, companies and textbooks has been inconsistent, and that lay people clean at most about 40 percent of tooth margins at the gumline.[1] The Tooth brushing article reports that no evidence shows any named technique to be superior to the others.[2]

chain: Less plaque at the gumline and gentler gum stimulation
Healthier-looking gum frame around the teeth
angle.text: People use gentle gumline brushing or massage to keep gum tissue looking firm and pink around the teeth, which frames a smile. The effects studied are gum health scores rather than appearance.

paras: Wikipedia describes the Stillman technique as similar to Bass but using vertical motions above and below the gum line, sometimes combined with Bass.[2] Other methods include modified Bass, with a rolling motion toward the biting edge, and Charters, with the brush angled about 45 degrees at the gumline.[2] Brushing can remove plaque up to about 1 mm below the gum line.[2]

General guidance reported includes avoiding hard pressure and horizontal scrubbing at the necks of teeth.[1] Harder brushes remove plaque more efficiently but stress teeth and gums more, and a 2011 study rated a medium-to-soft brush used longer as the best compromise.[1] The Tooth brushing article associates a sweeping technique with gingival recession and recommends simple techniques for children and Bass or modified Bass for adults.[2]

sections.h: Gum massage with oils and herbal products
paras: Oil gum massage is described in Indian dental research, and traditional oil massage of the gums is discussed in the context of oil pulling.[4] Commercial herbal gum massage powders have also been studied as adjuncts to mechanical gum treatment.[5]

A 2013 trial of 30 patients with fixed orthodontic appliances randomized them to scrubbing, modified Stillman or Bass brushing for nine months; plaque and gingival indices fell significantly in all groups.[3] A 2014 randomized trial had 32 participants massage their gums daily for three weeks with sesame, olive or coconut oil, or with chlorhexidine gel, and measured Streptococcus mutans counts plus plaque and gingival scores.[4] A 2013 trial of 75 people with gingivitis found that a herbal gum massage powder combined with scaling improved gingival and plaque indices compared with scaling alone, while the powder alone did not improve plaque control.[5] A 1948 study examined the effect of toothbrush massage on keratinization of the gingivae.[6]

timeline.event: Study published on the effect of toothbrush massage on keratinization of the gingivae.[6]
